column1: # The settings of the startup screen (LauncherActivity) and the in-game menu (vk/overlay.cpp): one row each, tab-separated:
#   key  tab  flags  default  values  names  label  help  needs
# key: the environment variable the game reads (launch.env); @name: a row that opens a page instead of holding a value;
#   =: a section heading (flag H), which shows only its label.
# values / names: '|'-separated, in the same order. Rows show in file order; tabs in order of first appearance.
# flags: L applies at once in the game (the rest are saved for the next start), Q also in the quick menu, X experimental,
#   D only when the app carries Turnip, S startup screen only, P opens a page (@ rows), H a section heading.
# Values starting with lsfg show only once the startup screen has made LSFG's shaders (Lsfg.java, vk/overlay.cpp).
# needs (optional): KEY=value|value: the row shows only while that setting has one of these values. A section must start
#   with a row that always shows. Help: one or two plain sentences, what it does and the trade-off; no figures that age.

column8: Runs the game as a handheld or as if docked to a TV. Docked looks sharper but works the GPU harder.
How detailed the 3D world is before it is fitted to the screen. Lower runs faster and cooler but looks softer. Sizes above the screen look smoother but need far more GPU power and memory.

How the picture is enlarged to fill the screen. FSR 1, NIS, SGSR and CAS rebuild edges and sharpen in different ways; Lanczos, Bicubic and Bilinear go from sharp to soft without extra sharpening; Nearest shows the pixels. MMPX, Super-xBR and ScaleFX come from pixel art and give a flatter, painted look. This only matters in handheld mode.
How crisp FSR 1 makes the picture. Stronger looks more detailed, but jagged edges stand out more; Off leaves the upscaled picture as it is.

How large ScaleFX draws the picture before it is fitted to the screen: the screen's own size, or 2× or 3× the game's picture (in handheld, 2560×1440 or 3840×2160). Screen size is the cheapest and suits most screens; 2× and 3× draw at a fixed size and then stretch or shrink it to fit, which costs more GPU time.

Smooths jagged edges in the world and leaves the HUD sharp. SMAA suits most players. SMAA T2x also calms flickering far-away edges, but fast movement can leave a faint trail. T2x needs docked mode; in handheld it acts like SMAA.
How hard SMAA looks for edges. High is enough for most scenes. Ultra finds fainter edges for a small GPU cost.
Builds each frame from several smaller ones, which smooths far-away edges better than SMAA and replaces it. Lights can shimmer, fast characters can smear, and it costs a lot of GPU time.
Keeps the ground and walls sharp when you see them at a shallow angle. Higher looks sharper and costs a little GPU time.
How sharp the sun’s shadows are, especially leaves on the ground. Higher values cost very little.
How far away the sun casts shadows. Near and Medium drop the shadows of distant hills and trees and lighten the load a little. Close shadows do not change.
The most pictures shown each second, counting generated ones. A lower limit saves power and heat. The game always runs at normal speed.
How often the screen updates. 120 Hz looks smoother when the frame rate is uneven. 60 Hz saves power. Some devices drop the screen to 60 Hz by themselves when they get very hot.

Adds pictures between the ones the game draws, so motion looks smoother. Homemade is the lightest. FSR 3.1 always doubles the frame rate. LSFG usually looks cleanest but uses the most GPU time, and needs your Lossless.dll, chosen in Tools > Lossless Scaling on the startup screen. Generation pauses if heat drops the screen to 60 Hz.

How many pictures frame generation adds. Fill adds one only when the game misses the frame rate limit. ×1.5 to ×4 hold the game to the limit divided by that number and generate the rest: higher numbers leave the game more time for each frame, but fast motion shows more errors.
How the game’s HUD looks with frame generation. Real frames stays sharp but moves at the game’s frame rate. Generated moves smoothly, but moving text can smear.
How closely LSFG follows motion. Lower uses less GPU time, but fast motion looks blurrier.
A lighter version of LSFG. It uses less GPU time but shows slightly more visual errors.
Up to the limit lets the game run as fast as the frame rate limit allows. Original keeps the Switch’s 30 to 40 frames per second.
Gives every frame the same time on screen. This can look steadier, but it adds input delay.
Choose which button does each action, such as jumping or attacking. Menu buttons follow Face buttons instead.
How A, B, X and Y match the Switch’s. By position uses the same places as a Switch, so the right-hand button is A. By label uses the letter printed on each button.
Which button symbols the game shows in its prompts. This changes the pictures only, never what a button does.
Aim by tilting the device, like the gyro controls on a Switch.
The game’s volume. The game is muted while this menu is open.
Shows the frame rate on screen, counting every picture shown.
Shows how long each frame takes, with a small graph. Red bars are too slow for 60 frames per second.
Shows how often the screen is updating right now. Some devices drop it to 60 Hz when they get very hot.
Shows the hottest of the CPU and GPU temperatures. Many devices slow themselves down when they get very hot.
Shows how many shaders are being built right now. A stutter while this is above zero is a shader being built.
Shows the graphics driver and its version.
Which corner of the screen the performance overlay sits in.
The graphics driver the game uses: your device’s own, the bundled Turnip driver for Adreno GPUs, or one from a .zip made for emulators. Each keeps its own shader cache.
Tells Android how long each frame takes, so it raises the CPU speed only as far as needed. This saves power and heat.
Keeps a video of the last 30 seconds, so a bug report can include it, even after a crash. It uses about 45 MB of storage and a little GPU time.
